newsitem.title: UK: Russia Eurobond need not hinge on Yeltsin's health.
newsitem.headline: Russia Eurobond need not hinge on Yeltsin's health.

text.p: The potential coincidence of Russia's plans to launch a Eurobond and heart surgery on President Boris Yeltsin has raised debate over the timing of the Eurobond roadshow which kicks off in November.
Yeltsin, aged 65, is impatient to have the operation as soon as possible, his wife Naina said on Thursday.

Most leading emerging market analysts said Yeltsin was not the sole concern in the launch of the Eurobond, which has already been delayed by other factors, among them the June presidential elections in Russia.

They said Russia would naturally suffer a period of uncertainty if Yeltsin died which would not make issuance easy. But the much-publicised Eurobond would still be feasible, even if its launch date had to be postponed again.
An Eastern European specialist in Frankfurt summed up the general market view: "Russia is larger than Yeltsin."
"There are more people than one who are competent to replace Yeltsin," he told Reuters.
If Yeltsin did die, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin would take his place and would have to hold an election within three months of Yeltsin's death, according to the constitution.

The Eurobond is Russia's first sovereign bond issue since the 1917 revolution and is expected to be a five-year deal for up to $500 million at a spread in the mid-300s basis points over five-year U.S. Treasuries, London bankers said.
J.P. Morgan and SBC Warburg will be joint lead managers.
The two investment banks said in a statement on Friday Russia will begin presentations on the economy in Asia, Europe and the U.S. on Monday November 11, ending in New York on Wednesday, November 20.
New issues traders believe there is enough investor interest to support the Eurobond, which will be a benchmark for other Russian borrowers to follow.

Moscow, St Petersburg and the Sverdlovsk region have all said they intend to tap the international capital market. There is thus pressure to launch Russia's Eurobond before year-end to pave the way for the others, new issues traders said.

A syndicate source close to the deal said: "As with any debut issue, we are sensitive to underlying conditions." He said at the end of the 10-day roadshow, they would assess market conditions and make a decision.
Another syndicate source close to the deal said recent country ratings would have taken into account political factors.

Moody's Investors Service has issued a prospective Ba2 sovereign ceiling on the foreign currency debt. Standard & Poor's Corp awarded Russia a BB-minus foreign currency debt rating. The ratings are below investment grade, but at the top end of market expectations.

Meanwhile an IMF delegation left Moscow this week without recommending the release of the latest tranche of a three-year loan. A Russian central bank statement said the IMF was worried about low Russian tax collection.
An emerging market analyst in London said the IMF withdrawal was bearish for Russian debt.
"But what makes the Eurobond valuable is the fact that Russian creditworthiness is essentially unaffected by short-term economic or political changes," the emerging market specialist said.
